title: Mara Ellison
biography_text:
Mara Ellison (born 14 May 1983) is an urban planner known for her work on compact city design, public transit integration, and community participation in land-use decisions. She has served as a senior urban planner in several mid-sized cities and has advised local governments on zoning reform, street design, and neighborhood redevelopment. Ellison’s work focuses on connecting housing, transportation, and public space in ways that support walkability and access to services.

Ellison was born in Harborview, a coastal industrial city. She grew up in a mixed-use neighborhood that included small factories, apartments, and corner shops. As a child, she observed heavy truck traffic, crowded sidewalks, and frequent flooding after storms. These conditions later influenced her interest in street safety and stormwater planning. She attended Harborview Public Schools and graduated from Harborview Central High School in 2001.

Ellison received a Bachelor of Arts in Geography and Urban Studies from Northport State University in 2005. During her undergraduate studies, she completed an internship with the Harborview Department of Planning, where she assisted with land-use maps and basic data entry for a new zoning code. She later earned a Master of Urban Planning from Lakefield Institute of Technology in 2007. Her graduate thesis examined the relationship between bus stop spacing and access to jobs in low-income neighborhoods.

After completing her education, Ellison accepted a position as a junior urban planner in the City of Northport Planning Division. In this role, she prepared staff reports for the planning commission, reviewed small development proposals, and updated the city’s land-use database. She also contributed to a corridor plan that recommended new bike lanes, bus shelters, and mixed-use zoning along a major arterial street.

In 2011, Ellison became an associate urban planner in the City of Clearbrook. There, she worked on the Clearbrook Comprehensive Plan, a long-range document guiding land use, transportation, parks, and utilities. She coordinated public workshops, created maps showing future land-use categories, and helped draft policies encouraging infill housing near transit stops. The plan introduced form-based zoning in selected corridors, which Ellison helped explain to residents and local business owners.

Ellison was promoted to senior urban planner in Clearbrook in 2014. As a senior urban planner, she led a small team responsible for neighborhood plans, transit-oriented development guidelines, and updates to the city’s zoning ordinance. She oversaw a station-area plan for a new light-rail extension, which included reduced parking requirements, wider sidewalks, and mixed-income housing targets. The plan also recommended ground-floor retail at key intersections to encourage active street life.

In 2017, Ellison joined the regional planning agency MetroRiver Council as a principal urban planner. At MetroRiver, she coordinated with multiple city planning departments, transit agencies, and county governments. Her work focused on aligning local zoning codes with the regional transportation plan. She helped create a regional toolkit for transit-oriented development that outlined model zoning language, density ranges, and street design standards around bus rapid transit and rail stations.

Ellison has been involved in several major projects across the MetroRiver region. She contributed to the Greenway Connections Plan, which proposed a network of off-street trails and green corridors linking neighborhoods, schools, and job centers. As an urban planner on the project, she analyzed land-use patterns near the proposed trails and recommended zoning changes to support small neighborhood centers and low-impact commercial uses along the routes. She also participated in the Downtown Reuse Study for the city of Redbridge, which examined the conversion of vacant office buildings into housing and community facilities.

A central theme in Ellison’s work as an urban planner is the integration of land use and transportation. She has supported bus-only lanes, safer pedestrian crossings, and reduced minimum parking requirements in areas with frequent transit service. Her reports often include side-by-side maps of transit access, housing density, and employment clusters, which she uses to identify gaps in service and opportunities for mixed-use development.

Ellison has taught part-time as an adjunct instructor in urban planning programs at Northport State University and Lakefield Institute of Technology. Her courses have covered zoning practice, site plan review, and public participation methods. In these roles, she has supervised student projects that analyze real neighborhoods and propose changes to land-use regulations, sidewalk networks, and transit access.

Ellison is a member of several professional organizations for urban planners. She has presented at conferences on topics including compact development, bus network redesign, and the use of geographic information systems in zoning analysis. She has written articles for planning journals on the effects of reduced parking requirements near transit and on methods for measuring walkability at the block level.

Throughout her career, Ellison has worked with community groups, business associations, and advocacy organizations. As an urban planner, she has facilitated public meetings, open houses, and design workshops. She has used visual tools such as 3D models, cross-section diagrams, and before-and-after streetscape images to explain proposed zoning changes and transportation projects. She is known among colleagues for her detailed staff reports and for connecting land-use recommendations to specific transportation and infrastructure policies.

Ellison continues to work as an urban planner at MetroRiver Council, focusing on regional housing targets and transit-supportive land-use policies. Her recent projects include updating the regional growth strategy to encourage more development near high-frequency transit corridors and revising model zoning codes to allow a wider range of housing types in established neighborhoods. She remains active in professional networks and contributes to training sessions for early-career urban planners.
